---
title: "Opportunity Sizing"
description: "How the World Model Graph sizes an opportunity and decomposes it into the drivers you can act on"
---

## Overview

**Opportunity Sizing** answers the question people actually ask about a
metric, which is not "where does this number vary?" but **"how do I improve
it, and by how much?"**

It lives in the **World Model Graph**, reached through the Globe icon in the
icon rail (a surface distinct from both the Context Graph and the
[Metric Tree](/guide/build/world-model/metric-tree)). When you open a measure
on the graph, Oxygen scans your data for segments that underperform a
benchmark, puts a dollar figure on each gap, and then lets you **drill** that
gap into its underlying drivers until you reach something specific enough to
act on.

The result is a ranked list of **addressable upside**, such as "mobile orders
run `$218.50/order` below in-store, and closing that gap is worth
`+$264.6k`," in which every number is backed by a statistical test and every
child in the breakdown provably sums back to its parent.

<Note>
Opportunity Sizing operates on the **semantic model**, reading your existing
[measures](/guide/build/semantic-model/measures),
[dimensions](/guide/build/semantic-model/dimensions), and the relationships
between [views](/guide/build/semantic-model/views), so you never define
opportunities anywhere yourself. The quality of the sizing depends directly on
how well your model is defined (see [What your model needs](#what-your-model-needs)).
</Note>

## The core idea: size on rates, not totals

An opportunity has two ingredients, a **gap** and a **volume**:

```
rate     = measure ÷ count            e.g. revenue per check
gap      = rate(segment) − rate(benchmark)
upside   = gap × volume(segment)
```

The single most important design decision is that Oxygen compares **per-unit
rates** and never raw totals.

If you compared raw sums, a segment sitting below another would mostly
reflect the fact that it is *smaller*, with fewer rows or a smaller market,
rather than that it *underperforms*. Comparing `revenue-per-check` instead of
`revenue` makes the comparison about performance, so that "smaller" never
reads as "worse," and multiplying the per-unit gap back by the segment's real
volume then turns it into an honest, addressable dollar figure.

<Warning>
Oxygen **refuses to guess** rather than emit a misleading number. If a measure
is an additive total (like a `sum`) but its view declares no `count` measure
from which to form a rate, the panel returns an empty result explaining why,
and it will not silently fall back to comparing totals. This is deliberate,
since a size-confounded number that looks precise is worse than no number at
all.
</Warning>

### Picking the benchmark

The benchmark is the bar every segment is measured against, and Oxygen picks
it from the data automatically:

| Number of segments | Benchmark | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fewer than 8 | `best_peer` | The actual top-performing segment |
| 8 or more | `p75` | The 75th-percentile performance level |

Crucially, the benchmark is defined as a **population filter** (`dim =
best_peer` or `dim IN (segments at or above p75)`) rather than as a bare
number, which is what lets the drill *query* the benchmark population later
instead of merely comparing against a fixed scalar.

### Three sizing modes

How a segment is weighted into a dollar figure depends on what the measure
supports:

| Weight basis | Applies to | Upside is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `rows` | Sum-like measures with a count denominator | `gap × count`, the fully honest path |
| `value_share` | Additive non-sum measures (`avg` / `min` / `max`) | Weighted by each segment's share of value |
| `equal` | Ratio measures | Equal weight per segment |

Only `rows` responses carry a directly addressable upside and get ranked in
the Opportunities list, although the other bases still power the drill
breakdown.

## Trustworthy numbers: the evidence gate

Any tool can find a "top lever" in *any* dataset, including one in which the
dimension is provably unrelated to the measure. Opportunity Sizing is
deliberately rigged against itself and corrects for the two ways a naive scan
fools itself.

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="Selection bias within a dimension" icon="magnifying-glass">
    The benchmark is the maximum (or P75) of the *same* segments being tested
    against it. If you draw a handful of values from pure noise, the largest
    one naturally sits well above the mean, so a fixed threshold would
    "discover" a leader in literally any dimension. Oxygen raises the bar by
    exactly that expected amount, so that noise does not clear it.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Multiple comparisons across the scan" icon="layer-group">
    A full scan makes on the order of a hundred comparisons once related
    entities are followed, and at a naive 5% per test, **five spurious levers
    per scan is the expected yield**. Oxygen therefore applies a Šidák
    correction across the whole scan family, so that 20 dimensions × 5
    segments requires a much higher bar of evidence than any single dimension
    would imply on its own.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

The test itself is **Welch's t-test** rather than a pooled-variance test,
because the benchmark is routinely the *thinner* of the two populations, and
a pooled estimate would understate the error exactly where it matters most.
With a two-row benchmark the effective degrees of freedom collapse, so the
gap has to be genuinely large to survive.

### Three outcomes, kept distinct

Oxygen never blurs "proven" with "plausible":

| Result | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| **Significant** | Kept and marked `gated: true`, as proven upside |
| **Not significant** | **Dropped**, and counted in `segments_dropped_as_noise` |
| **Can't tell** (no dispersion, `n < 2`, degenerate variance) | Kept but marked `gated: false`, meaning *ungated, not proven* |

The third row is the honest one. `gated: false` does **not** mean the gap is
fake; it means nobody could prove it real, and the panel never presents it as
proven upside. The skip reason also distinguishes *"everything I found was
noise"* from *"everything already matches the benchmark,"* because those are
different answers and you are entitled to know which one you got.

## Drill: decomposing the gap into drivers

Finding a gap is only half the job. **Drill** decomposes that gap
recursively, alternating between two kinds of split, until it reaches a
driver specific enough to act on:

- **Component splits** come from the measure's own formula (`revenue` →
  `entrée revenue` + `add-on revenue`).
- **Dimension splits** cut by an attribute (`add-on revenue` → by category).

The flow is recursive and domain-free, decomposing a per-unit gap through
structure until it reaches something specific.

### Two rules make the math honest

<Steps>
  <Step title="The denominator never changes">
    When the numerator is split by a dimension, the denominator is **not**
    filtered along with it, so `sides/order` means sides revenue divided by
    **all** of that segment's orders rather than by the sides count. If the
    denominator changed, the children would stop summing to the parent.
  </Step>
  <Step title="The benchmark is inherited, never re-picked">
    Every level compares the same two populations chosen at the root. If each
    child picked its own best peer, the children would stop summing to the
    parent and every percentage would be fiction.
  </Step>
</Steps>

### Why those rules matter

Given both rules, the decomposition becomes an **arithmetic identity** rather
than a fresh comparison at each level:

```
rate          = Σ children  (additive)   |  Π children  (multiplicative)
⇒ gap(rate)   = Σ gap(children)          |  log-share of the gap
⇒ upside      decomposes the same way
```

This is what earns a child the right to say **"91% of the parent gap."** The
figure is not an estimated or heuristic ranking but plain arithmetic, and the
children provably sum back to the parent at every level.

### What a drill looks like

```
mobile_app vs in_store             −218.5/order   +264.6k
├─ entrée/order      420 → 400       −20.0    9%     +24.2k
└─ add-on/order    342.4 → 143.9    −198.5   91%    +240.4k   ← follow
   ├─ sides/order   180 → 80        −100.0   46%    +121.1k   ← follow
   ├─ drinks/order   90 → 45         −45.0   21%
   └─ desserts       72 → 18.9       −53.1   24%
```

The last split (`sides/order = attach_rate × price_per_side`) answers whether
the gap comes from fewer sides or cheaper sides, which is the classic
volume-versus-value question, and it does so *inside* the decomposition
without any extra machinery.

### At each level, the drill:

1. **Enumerates candidates,** meaning the component edges from the measure's
   formula plus every dimension not already consumed higher up.
2. **Computes each child's gap and its share of the parent gap.**
3. **Ranks by concentration,** identifying which child holds the most of the
   gap.
4. **Shows all children with their shares** rather than just the winner, so
   siblings stay visible and "follow the max" remains a reading aid rather
   than a hidden selection.
5. **Recurses into the largest child.**
6. **Stops** when the next split fails the evidence gate, cannot be
   evidenced, has no candidates left, or reaches the maximum depth.

Every level renders its **stop reason**, and a level that could not be
evidence-checked is shown as *ungated* rather than as proven. The statistical
error budget is also split across depth, so that an N-level drill does not
quietly spend the full 5% error at every line.

## How to use it

<Steps>
  <Step title="Open the World Model Graph">
    Click the **Globe** icon in the icon rail to open the graph of your
    semantic model.
  </Step>
  <Step title="Select a measure">
    Click a measure node. Oxygen scans its segments when the node opens and,
    if it finds addressable upside, reveals an **Opportunities** section
    labeled *addressable upside · and where it comes from.*
  </Step>
  <Step title="Read the ranked segments">
    Each row shows the segment, its per-unit rate against the benchmark
    (`543.9 → 762.4 per order`), the dollar upside, and a proportion bar. You
    can use the copy button on a row to drop a ready-made investigation
    question into chat.
  </Step>
  <Step title="Drill into a gap">
    Expand a segment to decompose its gap. The drill runs **only on expand**,
    never when the node first opens, because it issues recursive queries
    against your warehouse. Follow the highlighted child downward until the
    stop reason tells you there is nothing left to prove.
  </Step>
</Steps>

## What your model needs

Opportunity Sizing is only as good as the semantic model underneath it, so
to get the most out of it:

- **Declare a `count` measure on the view.** Without a count denominator, a
  `sum` measure cannot be put on a per-unit basis, and Oxygen will refuse to
  size it rather than compare totals.
- **Model your metrics compositionally.** A measure defined as a sum or
  difference of same-view measures (`net_revenue = entrée_revenue +
  add_on_revenue`) gives the drill component edges to follow. Mirror trees
  work too, so a `gross_profit` tree that parallels `revenue` lets you drill
  margin the same way you drill revenue.
- **Keep dimensions meaningful to benchmark across.** A dimension in which
  being "higher" is a matter of arithmetic rather than performance (party
  size, for example, since a 6-top spends more than a 2-top by definition)
  will dominate the ranking without telling you anything, so prefer
  dimensions where a gap reflects something you can change.
- **Point it at measures where higher is better.** Both benchmark bases are
  top-end rates, so a segment below the benchmark is always read as upside.
  That reading is right for revenue, margin, or conversion but backwards for
  a cost, since a cost sum with a `count` on its view would rank the
  *cheapest* segment as the biggest opportunity. Size the revenue or profit
  side instead, and let the drill walk into the cost components rather than
  rooting a scan on a cost measure.

## Current scope

Opportunity Sizing is honest about what it can and cannot do, and about *why*
it cannot. What it refuses, it refuses **by design**, because sizing those
shapes would break the arithmetic identity the drill depends on. There is no
"not yet" bucket: a shape either sizes today or marks a permanent boundary,
and is never a quietly deferred promise.

**Works today**

- `sum` roots with a `count` on their view
- Additive same-view composites (`a + b − c`), including nested ones, where a
  composite whose child is itself a same-view composite flattens transitively
- Homogeneous `+`/`−` and `×`/`÷` expressions
- Dimension splits and cross-grain numerators

**Refused by design,** because Oxygen would rather decline than emit a number
that looks precise but isn't. These shapes break the
[sum-to-parent identity](#why-those-rules-matter), so no future work will
"fix" them without a different model:

| Won't size | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Ratio composites (`×` / `÷` roots) | A ratio isn't `measure ÷ count`, so it carries no addressable per-unit upside |
| Cross-view composites | The terms live at different grains, so there is no single denominator to put them on a common rate |
| Mixed expressions like `a + b*c` | Component edges are flat with no precedence, and a product's gap is a log-share that can't hang under an additive sum-to-parent rule |

Comparing a revenue drill against a margin drill side by side already works
today, since it is simply two drills read together. Ranking add-on leaves by
*profit* rather than *revenue* changes which leaf wins, so a true single-pass
co-ranking ("big revenue gap, thin margin") would be a presentation
improvement rather than an engine limitation, given that the engine already
sizes each measure on its own.

## In one paragraph

Oxygen sizes an opportunity as *(per-unit rate gap against a benchmark
segment) × volume*, working per unit rather than on raw totals so that
"smaller" never reads as "worse." The drill then decomposes that gap
recursively, alternating splits from the measure's own formula with splits by
dimension, while holding the denominator and the benchmark fixed all the way
down. Those two constraints turn the decomposition into an arithmetic
identity, which is what lets a child legitimately claim "91% of the parent
gap" and guarantees that children sum back to the parent. The drill stops
when the evidence gate can no longer prove the next split, and it always
tells you why it stopped.
